overview: Partition pruning is an optimization where Spark skips reading entire partitions (directories of files) at read time when a query filter on a partition column rules them out.
It relies on Hive-style directory partitioning, where data is physically laid out in folders named by partition-column values, so Spark can use the directory path to eliminate irrelevant data.
Dynamic partition pruning (DPP), introduced in Spark 3.0, extends this to joins, pruning the fact table's partitions at runtime based on values from the dimension side.
learningObjectives: Understand how partition pruning skips irrelevant partitions using partition-column predicates to cut I/O.
Learn the role of Hive-style directory partitioning and how Spark prunes at the directory level.
Distinguish static partition pruning from dynamic partition pruning (DPP) and from predicate pushdown.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: Partition pruning is a query optimization in which the engine eliminates partitions from the scan plan whose partition-column values cannot satisfy the query's predicates, thereby avoiding reading those partitions' files entirely. Static partition pruning resolves prunable partitions from literal predicates at planning time; dynamic partition pruning resolves them at runtime from the result of another part of the query (typically the filtered dimension side of a join).
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Imagine a filing cabinet where each drawer is labeled by year (2021, 2022, 2023). If someone asks for records from 2023, you only open the 2023 drawer and ignore the others entirely. Partition pruning is Spark opening only the relevant drawers (directories) instead of reading every file in the cabinet, which saves enormous amounts of reading work.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Directory-based partitioning originated with Apache Hive, which organized table data into subdirectories named by partition column values. Spark adopted this Hive-style layout for its data sources. Static partition pruning has long been part of Spark SQL's Catalyst optimizer. Dynamic Partition Pruning was a major feature added in Spark 3.0 to optimize star-schema joins, allowing the large fact table to be pruned using filters applied to small dimension tables at runtime.

whyItMatters.business: Pruning slashes the amount of data scanned, directly reducing query latency and cloud scan costs (e.g., bytes read from S3), making analytics cheaper and dashboards faster.
whyItMatters.engineering: It lets engineers design tables whose physical layout matches common query filters so the engine reads only relevant data, a foundational technique for performant data lakes.
whyItMatters.scalability: As datasets grow to petabytes, scanning everything becomes infeasible; pruning keeps query cost proportional to the data actually needed rather than total table size.
whyItMatters.cost: On pay-per-scan engines and object stores, reading fewer partitions means fewer bytes read and fewer requests, often cutting query cost by orders of magnitude.
whyItMatters.reliability: Reading less data reduces memory pressure, shuffle volume, and runtime variability, making queries more predictable and less prone to resource exhaustion.

coreComponents.name: Hive-style Partition Layout
coreComponents.definition: A directory structure where data files are stored in folders named partition_col=value (e.g., /events/dt=2023-01-01/).
coreComponents.purpose: To encode partition-column values in the path so the engine can decide which directories to read without opening files.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Physically separate data by partition value so pruning can operate at the directory level.

coreComponents.name: Partition Filter / Predicate
coreComponents.definition: A query condition on a partition column (e.g., WHERE dt = '2023-01-01') that the optimizer uses to select partitions.
coreComponents.purpose: To identify which partitions can possibly contain matching rows and prune the rest.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Be expressed on the partition column so Catalyst can map it to specific directories.
coreComponents.examples: df.filter(col("dt") == "2023-01-01") prunes all other date directories.

coreComponents.name: Dynamic Partition Pruning (DPP) Subquery
coreComponents.definition: A runtime mechanism that broadcasts the distinct filtered values from the dimension side of a join to prune the fact table's partitions.
coreComponents.purpose: To prune partitions in joins where the filter is not a literal but derived from another table.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Compute the set of join-key values surviving the dimension filter and apply them as a partition filter on the fact table at runtime.
coreComponents.examples: Joining a partitioned sales fact with a date dimension filtered to one quarter prunes sales to that quarter's partitions.

internalWorking: When a query has a predicate on a partition column, Catalyst recognizes it as a partition filter and consults the table's partition metadata (directory structure or metastore) to determine the matching partitions.
Only the file paths under matching partition directories are added to the scan's list of files to read; all other partitions are excluded before any data is read, so their files are never opened.

For dynamic partition pruning, the optimizer inserts a subquery that, at runtime, collects the distinct join-key values surviving the dimension-side filter and pushes them as a dynamic partition filter onto the fact-table scan, pruning partitions based on values known only after the dimension is read.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Query Predicate on Partition Column -> Catalyst identifies partition filter -> Match against partition metadata/directories -> Scan reads only matching partition directories -> (DPP) Runtime dimension values -> Dynamic filter prunes fact partitions
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. A table /events is partitioned by dt with directories dt=2023-01-01, dt=2023-01-02, ... dt=2023-12-31.
3. Catalyst recognizes dt as a partition column and maps the predicate to the single directory dt=2023-06-15.
4. The file scan list includes only files under that one directory; the other 364 directories are never read.
5. Spark reads a tiny fraction of the table, cutting I/O dramatically compared to a full scan.

keyTerminology.meaning: A column whose distinct values define the directory partitioning of a table on disk.
keyTerminology.importance: Predicates on partition columns are what enable pruning; non-partition columns cannot prune partitions.

keyTerminology.meaning: Pushing filters down to the data source/file format so it skips rows or row groups using file statistics.
keyTerminology.importance: Often confused with partition pruning; pushdown operates inside files (row groups), pruning operates on whole partitions/directories.

keyTerminology.meaning: Runtime pruning of a fact table's partitions using filtered values from a joined dimension table.
keyTerminology.importance: Enables pruning for star-schema joins where the filter is indirect, a major Spark 3.0 optimization.

importantConcepts.explanation: Static pruning happens at planning time from literal predicates (WHERE dt = '2023-06-15'). Dynamic pruning happens at runtime when the filter value is unknown until another query branch executes, such as the filtered dimension side of a join supplying the values to prune the fact table.

Too few partitions limit pruning effectiveness; too many (high-cardinality partition columns) create the small-files problem and huge metadata. Good partition columns are low-to-moderate cardinality and frequently filtered, like date or region.

variationsAndTypes: **Static Partition Pruning:** Resolved at planning time from literal predicates on partition columns.
**Dynamic Partition Pruning (DPP):** Resolved at runtime using filtered join-key values from a dimension table.
**Single-column pruning:** Filtering on one partition column (e.g., dt).
**Multi-column / nested pruning:** Filtering on several partition columns of a multi-level directory layout (e.g., year=/month=/day=).
advantages: **Massive I/O Reduction:** Skips reading entire partitions, often eliminating the vast majority of data scanned.
**Lower Cost:** Fewer bytes read from object storage directly reduces scan and request costs.
**Faster Queries:** Less data to read, shuffle, and process shortens runtimes substantially.
**Works for Joins via DPP:** Dynamic pruning extends benefits to star-schema joins automatically.
disadvantages: **Requires Good Partitioning:** Only works if the table is partitioned by columns matching common filters.
**No Help for Non-partition Filters:** Predicates on non-partition columns cannot prune partitions.
**Over-partitioning Risks:** High-cardinality partition columns cause small files and metadata bloat.
**DPP Conditions:** Dynamic pruning requires specific plan shapes (e.g., broadcastable dimension) and the feature enabled to trigger.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use partition pruning by partitioning tables on low-to-moderate cardinality columns that are frequently used in filters (e.g., date, region, tenant). Rely on DPP for star-schema joins where a small dimension filters a large partitioned fact.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid partitioning on high-cardinality columns (e.g., user_id) that would create millions of tiny directories; in such cases use file-level techniques like Parquet predicate pushdown, bucketing, or Z-ordering instead.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Think of a multi-floor library where books are shelved by year and then by month. To find a June 2023 article, the librarian walks straight to the 2023 floor and the June shelf, ignoring every other floor and shelf. Partition pruning is Spark walking straight to the right directories instead of scanning the entire library, drastically cutting the search effort.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Partition pruning and predicate pushdown are the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Partition pruning skips whole partitions (directories) using partition-column predicates before reading any files. Predicate pushdown happens within files, using row-group statistics (min/max) to skip data inside the files that are read. They are complementary, not identical.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Filtering on any column lets Spark prune partitions.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Only filters on the partition column(s) prune partitions. A filter on a non-partition column cannot eliminate directories; it can at best benefit from predicate pushdown within the files that are scanned.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Pruning is essential at scale: it keeps query cost proportional to the partitions queried rather than total table size, so petabyte tables remain queryable when partitioned on commonly-filtered columns.
productionConsiderations.reliability: By reading far less data, pruning reduces memory pressure and shuffle volume, lowering the chance of OOM and producing more predictable, reliable query performance.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Pruning reduces the data footprint of each task, shrinking the work that must be recomputed on task failure and making retries cheaper.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Verify pruning via the physical plan: look for PartitionFilters in the FileScan node and a reduced number of files/partitions read in the Spark UI; absence indicates pruning is not happening.
productionConsiderations.security: Partition layout can align with data isolation (e.g., partition by tenant or region), and pruning ensures queries touch only the relevant partitions, though access control must still be enforced separately.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: On pay-per-scan and object-store pricing, pruning is one of the highest-leverage cost optimizations, often reducing bytes scanned by orders of magnitude; design partition columns around frequent filter predicates.
productionConsiderations.performance: Effective pruning depends on partition column choice (low cardinality, frequently filtered) and avoiding casts/functions on partition columns in predicates that defeat pruning; for joins, enable and verify DPP.

codeExamples.title: Writing and Reading a Partitioned Table to Enable Pruning
codeExamples.overview: Shows how to write data partitioned by a column and then confirm static partition pruning via the physical plan.
codeExamples.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("PruningDemo").getOrCreate()

# Write Hive-style partitioned data: creates directories like dt=2023-06-15/
events.write.mode("overwrite").partitionBy("dt").parquet("/data/events")

# Read and filter on the partition column to trigger pruning
df = spark.read.parquet("/data/events")
filtered = df.filter(df.dt == "2023-06-15")

# Inspect the plan: look for PartitionFilters in the FileScan
filtered.explain()
codeExamples.breakdown: partitionBy("dt") writes data into directories named dt=<value>. The filter on dt is recognized as a partition filter, so explain() shows PartitionFilters: [dt = 2023-06-15] in the FileScan and reads only that directory.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: A physical plan whose FileScan node lists PartitionFilters: [isnotnull(dt), (dt = 2023-06-15)] and reads only the dt=2023-06-15 partition, not the whole table.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Filtering on a non-partition column does not prune. Applying a function/cast to the partition column (e.g., to_date(dt)) can prevent the optimizer from matching directories.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Partition on low-to-moderate cardinality columns that are commonly filtered. Verify PartitionFilters appears in explain() and that the number of files read drops accordingly.

codeExamples.title: Dynamic Partition Pruning in a Star-Schema Join
codeExamples.overview: Demonstrates DPP, where filtering a small date dimension prunes partitions of a large partitioned sales fact at runtime.
codeExamples.code:
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.optimizer.dynamicPartitionPruning.enabled", "true")

# sales is large and partitioned by date_id; date_dim is small
sales = spark.read.parquet("/data/sales")          # partitioned by date_id
date_dim = spark.read.parquet("/data/date_dim")

# Filter the small dimension; DPP pushes the surviving date_ids to prune sales
result = (sales.join(date_dim, "date_id")
               .where(date_dim.quarter == "2023-Q2"))

result.explain()  # Look for dynamicpruningexpression on the sales scan
codeExamples.breakdown: The dimension date_dim is filtered to one quarter. With DPP enabled, Spark computes the set of date_id values for that quarter at runtime and applies them as a dynamic partition filter on the partitioned sales scan, so only matching partitions are read.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: An explain plan where the sales FileScan shows a dynamicpruningexpression / PartitionFilters referencing the broadcast subquery, and far fewer sales partitions are read than the full table.
codeExamples.commonIssues: DPP may not trigger if it is disabled, if the dimension side is not broadcastable, or if the fact table is not partitioned on the join key. AQE and broadcast settings influence whether it fires.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Ensure the fact table is partitioned by the join key, keep the dimension small enough to broadcast, and enable spark.sql.optimizer.dynamicPartitionPruning.enabled (default true in Spark 3.x).

codeExamples.title: Partition Pruning vs Predicate Pushdown
codeExamples.overview: Contrasts pruning a partition column with pushing a predicate on a non-partition column down to Parquet row groups.
codeExamples.code:
df = spark.read.parquet("/data/events")  # partitioned by dt

# Partition pruning: dt is the partition column -> skips directories
q1 = df.filter(df.dt == "2023-06-15")
q1.explain()  # PartitionFilters: [dt = 2023-06-15]

# Predicate pushdown: amount is a regular column inside the files
q2 = df.filter(df.amount > 1000)
q2.explain()  # PushedFilters: [GreaterThan(amount,1000)] (no partition pruning)
codeExamples.breakdown: For q1, dt is the partition column, so the plan shows PartitionFilters and entire directories are skipped. For q2, amount is a normal column, so the plan shows PushedFilters; Parquet uses row-group min/max stats to skip data inside files, but no directories are pruned.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: q1's plan contains PartitionFilters and reads one directory; q2's plan contains PushedFilters on amount and still scans all partitions but skips non-matching row groups within files.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Confusing the two: expecting a filter on amount to prune partitions. Predicate pushdown effectiveness depends on data being sorted/clustered so row-group stats are selective.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Combine both: partition on commonly-filtered low-cardinality columns (pruning) and sort/Z-order by high-cardinality filter columns so pushdown via row-group stats is effective.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: An analytics team queries a multi-terabyte sales table, but most queries only need a single day or quarter of data. Full-table scans make queries slow and expensive on their pay-per-scan object store, and the bill is climbing as data accumulates.
endToEndExample.inputData: A 10TB sales fact table written as Parquet, plus a small date dimension table. Queries typically filter to a specific date range or join to the date dimension filtered by quarter.
endToEndExample.architecture: The sales table is written partitioned by date_id (Hive-style directories), and queries either filter directly on date_id (static pruning) or join the small date dimension filtered by quarter (dynamic pruning). Spark 3.x runs with DPP enabled.
processingSteps: 1. Write the sales fact partitioned by date_id so each day is a directory.
2. For point-in-time queries, filter sales.date_id == target so static pruning reads only that day's directory.
3. For quarter-level reports, join sales to the date dimension and filter the dimension by quarter; DPP prunes sales partitions at runtime.
4. Inspect explain() to confirm PartitionFilters / dynamicpruningexpression appear.
5. Run the report and observe the reduced bytes scanned.
endToEndExample.output: Query results computed by reading only the relevant date partitions of the 10TB table, typically a few gigabytes instead of the full table.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Check the Spark UI scan metrics for files/bytes read and confirm only the expected partitions are scanned; verify PartitionFilters or dynamic pruning expressions in the physical plan for each query.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: If a query unexpectedly scans the whole table, inspect the plan for missing PartitionFilters (often caused by functions/casts on the partition column or DPP not triggering) and rewrite the predicate or ensure the fact is partitioned on the join key.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Query latency and scan cost drop by orders of magnitude because Spark reads only the needed partitions. Static pruning handles direct date filters and DPP handles dimension-driven quarter reports, keeping cost proportional to data actually queried rather than total table size.

industryUseCases.problem: Petabyte-scale event tables made full scans prohibitively slow and costly for time-windowed analytics.
industryUseCases.solution: Partition tables by date so queries filtering on date prune to only the relevant day/month directories, reading a tiny fraction of the data.
industryUseCases.benefits: Order-of-magnitude reductions in bytes scanned and query latency, with substantial cloud storage cost savings.

industryUseCases.problem: Queries scanned data across all tenants, wasting I/O and risking cross-tenant performance impact.
industryUseCases.solution: Partition large tables by tenant and date so tenant- and time-scoped queries prune to the relevant partitions only.
industryUseCases.benefits: Faster, cheaper per-tenant queries and cleaner data isolation aligned with the physical layout.

industryUseCases.problem: BI reports joined a huge partitioned sales fact with small date and store dimensions, but full fact scans were slow.
industryUseCases.solution: Enable dynamic partition pruning so filters on the small dimensions prune the fact table's partitions at runtime.
industryUseCases.benefits: Star-schema joins read only relevant fact partitions, dramatically speeding up BI dashboards without manual query rewrites.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Partition pruning is the primary mechanism that keeps query cost proportional to data queried rather than total table size, enabling petabyte tables to remain interactive when partitioned on frequently-filtered, low-cardinality columns such as date.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: By limiting each query's data footprint, pruning shrinks the amount of work per task and therefore the cost of recomputation on failure, making retries cheaper and jobs more resilient.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Reduced scan volume lowers cluster load and contention, helping maintain responsiveness for concurrent queries on shared clusters and reducing the chance of resource saturation.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: A clear partition layout simplifies selective recovery and backfills: individual partitions can be reprocessed or restored independently without touching the whole table.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Choose partition columns matching common filters with low-to-moderate cardinality, avoid functions/casts on partition columns in predicates (which defeat pruning), combine pruning with sorting/Z-ordering for in-file pushdown, and enable/verify DPP for star-schema joins.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: On pay-per-scan engines and object stores, pruning is among the highest-leverage cost optimizations, frequently cutting bytes scanned by orders of magnitude; design the partition scheme around the most common and selective query predicates.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Aligning partitions with isolation boundaries (tenant, region) helps queries touch only authorized data ranges, but partition pruning is a performance feature and must be paired with proper access controls, not relied on for security.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Confirm pruning in the physical plan (PartitionFilters, dynamicpruningexpression) and track files/bytes read in the Spark UI; a sudden rise in bytes scanned signals broken pruning, often from predicate rewrites or schema changes.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Validate that partition directory values are consistent and correctly typed; malformed or mistyped partition values can be silently excluded or prevent pruning, leading to wrong or slow results.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log per-query bytes/files scanned and alert when scans exceed expected thresholds for partitioned tables, which usually indicates pruning regressions or queries missing partition predicates.

recommendedPractices: **Partition on filter columns:** Choose low-to-moderate cardinality columns that queries commonly filter on, such as date or region.
**Avoid functions on partition columns in predicates:** Filter directly (dt = '2023-06-15'), not with casts/functions that defeat pruning.
**Verify pruning in the plan:** Always check explain() for PartitionFilters or dynamicpruningexpression.
**Enable DPP for star schemas:** Keep dimensions broadcastable and the fact partitioned on the join key so dynamic pruning fires.
engineeringStandards: Document the partition scheme of each table and the queries it is designed to serve.
Avoid high-cardinality partition columns that create the small-files problem.
Include explain-plan checks in code review or tests to ensure pruning is preserved.
designRecommendations: Use multi-level partitioning (e.g., year/month/day) only when queries filter at those granularities.
Combine partitioning (pruning) with sorting or Z-ordering by secondary filter columns (pushdown) for layered I/O reduction.
Keep dimension tables small enough to broadcast so DPP can prune fact partitions.
namingConventions: Use clear partition column names that match query predicates (e.g., dt, event_date, region).
Follow the Hive-style key=value directory convention consistently across tables.
documentationStandards: Document which columns each table is partitioned by and why.
Record expected pruning behavior and typical bytes-scanned for common queries.
Note any reliance on DPP and the configs/conditions required for it to trigger.
testingStrategies: Assert that explain() plans for representative queries contain PartitionFilters.
Test DPP joins to confirm dynamicpruningexpression appears and fact partitions are pruned.
Monitor bytes/files scanned in tests to catch pruning regressions after schema or query changes.

commonMistakes.mistake: Applying a function or cast to the partition column in the filter.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Engineers write predicates like to_date(dt) = '2023-06-15' or cast(dt as date) = ... out of habit.
commonMistakes.impact: The optimizer can no longer map the predicate to directory values, so pruning is disabled and the whole table is scanned.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Filter on the partition column directly with a matching literal type (dt = '2023-06-15') so Catalyst can prune directories.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Choosing a column like user_id or timestamp-to-the-second assuming finer partitioning means more pruning.
commonMistakes.impact: Creates millions of tiny directories and files, causing the small-files problem, huge metadata, and slow planning that outweigh pruning benefits.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Partition on low-to-moderate cardinality columns (date, region); use bucketing or Z-ordering for high-cardinality filter columns instead.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting filters on non-partition columns to prune partitions.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Confusing partition pruning with predicate pushdown.
commonMistakes.impact: Queries scan all partitions because the filter column is not the partition column, leading to surprise full-table scans.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Understand that only partition-column predicates prune directories; non-partition filters rely on in-file predicate pushdown, which still reads all partitions.

comparisonSection.explanation: Partition pruning skips entire partitions (directories of files) before any file is opened, using predicates on partition columns. Predicate pushdown happens inside the files that are read, using row-group/footer statistics (min/max) to skip data within files. Pruning eliminates directories; pushdown eliminates row groups inside scanned files. They are complementary.

Static pruning resolves prunable partitions at planning time from literal predicates (WHERE dt = '2023-06-15'). Dynamic pruning resolves them at runtime, using the distinct join-key values that survive a filter on a joined dimension table to prune the partitioned fact table on the fly.

comparisonSection.optionB: Predicate Pushdown (works on any columnar file)
comparisonSection.explanation: Partition pruning requires the table to be physically partitioned (Hive-style directories) on the filter column. Predicate pushdown works on any columnar format (e.g., Parquet/ORC) regardless of partitioning, as long as the format stores column statistics; it does not require directory partitioning.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is partition pruning in Spark?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Partition pruning is an optimization where Spark skips reading entire partitions (directories) when a query's filter on a partition column rules them out. For a table partitioned by date, filtering on a single date reads only that date's directory and ignores the rest, cutting I/O dramatically.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Emphasize skipping whole directories based on partition-column predicates and the resulting I/O savings.

beginnerQuestions.question: What table layout is needed for partition pruning to work?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Hive-style directory partitioning, where data is stored in folders named partition_col=value (e.g., dt=2023-06-15). Spark uses the directory path to know which partitions can match the filter and reads only those.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Tie pruning to the physical partitionBy layout; without it there are no partition directories to prune.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is the difference between partition pruning and predicate pushdown?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Partition pruning skips entire partitions/directories before reading any files, using predicates on partition columns. Predicate pushdown happens inside the files that are scanned, using row-group min/max statistics to skip data within files. Pruning works at the directory level; pushdown works at the row-group level. They complement each other.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: This is a classic confusion. Stress directory-level vs in-file row-group level, and that both can apply together.

intermediateQuestions.question: How can a poorly written predicate disable partition pruning?
intermediateQuestions.answer: If you wrap the partition column in a function or cast (e.g., to_date(dt) = '2023-06-15'), the optimizer cannot map the predicate to directory values and falls back to a full scan. Filtering directly on the partition column with a matching literal preserves pruning.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Shows practical awareness; interviewers like the function-on-partition-column gotcha.

advancedQuestions.question: Explain dynamic partition pruning and when it triggers.
advancedQuestions.answer: DPP (Spark 3.0+) prunes a large partitioned fact table at runtime using filtered values from a joined dimension. When a small dimension is filtered and joined to a fact partitioned on the join key, Spark inserts a subquery that computes the surviving join-key values and pushes them as a dynamic partition filter onto the fact scan. It typically triggers when the dimension side is broadcastable, the fact is partitioned on the join key, and spark.sql.optimizer.dynamicPartitionPruning.enabled is true.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Demonstrates star-schema knowledge and the runtime nature plus the trigger conditions (broadcast, partition key, config).

advancedQuestions.question: How does partition pruning interact with object-store query cost and scalability?
advancedQuestions.answer: On pay-per-scan engines and object stores, cost is driven by bytes read and requests. Pruning reduces both by reading only relevant partition directories, keeping cost proportional to the data actually queried instead of total table size. This makes pruning the highest-leverage optimization for petabyte tables, but it depends on choosing partition columns that match common, selective filter predicates without over-partitioning into tiny files.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Connects pruning to cost/scalability and the partition-cardinality trade-off, the deeper design angle.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: A query on a date-partitioned table that filters to a single day is unexpectedly scanning the whole table. How do you diagnose and fix it?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: A full scan on a partitioned table means pruning isn't happening. Check explain() for PartitionFilters. Common causes: a function/cast on the partition column, a type mismatch with the partition value, or filtering on a non-partition column. Fix the predicate to reference the partition column directly with the right literal type.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Run explain() and look for missing PartitionFilters. Most likely the predicate wraps the partition column in a function/cast or uses a mismatched type; rewrite it as dt = '2023-06-15' so Catalyst maps it to the directory. Confirm the bytes/files scanned drop in the Spark UI.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design the storage layout for a petabyte-scale event table queried by date range and joined to small dimensions, optimizing for scan cost.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Write the fact table as Parquet partitioned by date (and possibly a coarse secondary key like region) so date-range queries prune directories. Sort/Z-order within partitions by high-cardinality filter columns to enable in-file predicate pushdown. Keep dimensions small/broadcastable and enable DPP so dimension filters prune fact partitions in joins.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Finer partitioning improves pruning but risks small files and metadata bloat; coarser partitioning reduces files but prunes less. Partitioning helps directory-level skipping, while pushdown handles in-file skipping; combining both layers the savings.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Pick partition granularity (e.g., daily) so each partition stays at a healthy file size as volume grows. Use bucketing or Z-ordering for high-cardinality predicates. Monitor bytes scanned and adjust the partition scheme if queries shift, ensuring DPP continues to fire for star-schema joins.

Filter directly on the partition column with a matching literal type.
Combine pruning (directories) with pushdown (row groups) and Z-ordering for layered I/O savings.

keyTakeaways: Partition pruning skips reading entire partition directories at read time using predicates on partition columns, drastically cutting I/O and cost.
It requires Hive-style directory partitioning (key=value folders); only filters on the partition column can prune, and functions/casts on that column disable pruning.

Static pruning resolves partitions from literals at planning time, while dynamic partition pruning (Spark 3.0+) prunes a partitioned fact table at runtime using filtered values from a joined dimension.
Partition pruning is distinct from predicate pushdown: pruning skips whole directories, pushdown skips row groups inside the files that are read, and the two combine for layered savings.
Choose low-to-moderate cardinality, frequently-filtered partition columns (like date) to maximize pruning while avoiding the small-files problem from over-partitioning.
